issues.description: The problem statement and solution expect a class named Meal (with constructor Meal(String, String[])) but the template repository contains an Order class (src/de/tum/cit/ase/Order.java) and an empty Meal.java. The template's Main also uses Order. This name/type mismatch (Order vs Meal) will confuse students: they may implement Meal as required by the spec but find an existing Order class in the template, or follow the template and implement behavior for Order which will not match the exercise description or the solution. The absence of a proper Meal class in the template prevents students from following the specified design and signatures.
issues.suggestedFix: Update the template to match the problem statement: provide a Meal.java skeleton with the constructor Meal(String, String[]) and remove (or rename) the extraneous Order.java. Also update the template Main to reference Meal rather than Order. Alternatively, if Order is intended, update the problem statement and solution to refer to Order consistently. This will align types and prevent confusion.

issues.description: The problem statement and solution refer to the same domain entity as 'Meal', but the template repository provides an 'Order' class (and an empty Meal.java). This creates a naming mismatch: students are told to implement behavior around a Meal entity, yet the starter code exposes an Order class and an empty Meal file. The inconsistent identifiers (Meal vs Order) for the same conceptual entity can confuse students about which class to use or modify.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the identifier across artifacts. Either rename the template's Order class to Meal (updating references in Main and elsewhere) or provide a properly implemented Meal class in the template and remove/rename Order. Ensure the problem statement, template, and solution consistently use the same class name (Meal) so students can directly map requirements to the starter code.
